transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I just... I haven’t been able to get back to myself since my friend was killed. Everyone around me seemed to think that with time it would soften, or I’d be able to make some kind of peace with it, but it hasn’t gone that way for me.

It’s like I’m carrying this constant mix of guilt and fear and anger all the time. Some days one of them is louder than the others, but they’re always there in the background. I keep thinking I should be handling it better, especially at my age, but I’m not. I’m just tired of feeling like this hasn’t eased at all.
Do you find yourself re-living the event or having intrusive thoughts, memories, or nightmares about your friend's death?

Yes. I do. It’s not always like I’m choosing to think about it, you know? It just… arrives. Something ordinary will set it off, and suddenly I’m right back there in my mind.

A crosswalk signal is one of the worst things. That little beeping or the change in the light, and before I even realize what’s happening, I can see her stepping off the curb. Or if I hear a truck coming up behind me or going past—just that low growl of the engine—it makes my whole body react, and the picture comes back so sharply. Even something as silly as seeing a walking-tour map can do it, because it reminds me of where we were and what we were doing, and then the whole scene just unfolds in my head before I can stop it.

It feels very vivid, not like a normal memory where you can keep some distance from it. It’s more like my mind throws me into it, and I’m seeing that moment again. I try to push it away, but by the time I notice it happening, I’m already there.
Do you find yourself avoiding places, people, or activities that remind you of your friend or the incident?

Yes. Very much so. I don’t really like admitting how much I’ve rearranged my life around it, but I have.

I go out of my way to avoid that intersection now. I mean, I will take a longer route, sometimes a ridiculously longer one, just so I don’t have to be anywhere near it. Even if I’m in a car and not walking, I still don’t want to pass it. I tell myself it’s just practical, or that there’s too much traffic there anyway, but the truth is I can’t bear seeing it.

And I’ve stopped signing up for most walking tours and city tours, things I actually used to enjoy. I used to like being out, learning things, walking with a group, having a little structure to the day. Now even the idea of it makes me tense, because I’m afraid the route will go near that place or someone will start talking about pedestrian safety or accidents or what happened there.

I’ve also avoided safety meetings and community discussions, which sounds strange because part of me thinks maybe I should go, maybe I should be involved somehow. But I can’t sit through conversations that circle back to that incident. Once people start talking about that intersection, or trucks, or what should have been done differently, I just feel like I can’t stay in the room. So I don’t go. I’ve pulled back from a lot of things that even come close to reminding me of it.
Do you find that you have persistent feelings of guilt, fear, or anger related to the incident or your friend's death, and if so, how do these feelings affect your daily life?

Yes. That’s really the center of it, I think. Since she was killed, I’ve been living with this constant mix of guilt and fear and anger, and it just hasn’t eased the way people seemed to think it would. People say time helps, and maybe it does for some things, but for me it feels like it’s all still sitting right under the surface.

The guilt is there because I keep wondering what I could have done differently, even if part of me knows I can’t go back and change anything. The fear is there because the world doesn’t feel as ordinary or safe as it used to. And the anger… I’m angry that it happened, angry that she’s gone, angry that my life is now organized around something so awful.

It affects my days because I don’t feel relaxed the way I used to. I wake up already carrying it, and even when I’m doing normal things, it’s like there’s this heaviness underneath everything. I try to function, but emotionally I feel worn down. It’s exhausting to be this tense and upset for this long.
Have you noticed that you feel more depressed, irritable, or unable to enjoy things you used to like since your friend’s death?

Yes… I have. It’s hard to explain, because it’s not always crying or feeling obviously sad every minute. It’s more like the color has gone out of things.

I used to be someone who really planned things. I’d sit with seed catalogs and sketch out my garden beds, thinking about which flowers would go where, what would bloom first, how it would look from the kitchen window. I used to love that. And quilting with the ladies — that was something I looked forward to, not just the sewing but the talking, the little jokes, seeing what everyone was working on. Theater outings, too. I’d get excited about those. I’d make a whole evening of it.

And book club… I used to argue happily at book club. Not in a mean way, just, you know, getting worked up about a character or whether the ending made sense. I enjoyed having opinions. I enjoyed being part of things.

Now I look at those same things on the calendar and I feel almost nothing. Sometimes I stare at them like they belong to someone else, or someone I used to be. I know they should matter to me. I know I used to care. But there’s this blankness, or distance, and I just don’t have that spark for them anymore.
Do you find yourself being unusually watchful or easily startled since your friend's death?

Yes. Especially near traffic. I didn’t used to be like that — I mean, I was careful, of course, everyone is careful crossing a street — but now it’s like my whole body goes on duty.

If I’m anywhere near a road, I’m watching everything. Every truck, every curb, every person stepping off the sidewalk. I’ll notice if someone is looking down at their phone, or if a truck seems too close to the corner, or if the light is changing and someone looks like they might hurry across. It feels almost like I’m responsible for catching the danger before it happens again, even though I know, logically, I can’t control all of that.

I’ll stand there and scan back and forth, back and forth, and I can feel myself getting tense. Sometimes I’m not even the one crossing — I might just be nearby — but I’m still watching like I have to be ready. It’s exhausting, honestly, because a simple walk or even waiting near a street doesn’t feel simple anymore.
Have these feelings of emptiness or lack of interest lasted most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Yes… yes, it has. Not just a bad afternoon here and there. It’s been there most days, and for most of the day, for longer than two weeks. Honestly, it feels like it’s become the background of my life.

I’ll see things on the calendar that used to make me feel like myself — planning the garden beds, quilting with the ladies, going to the theater, book club — and I just feel this flatness. I used to look forward to all of that. I’d fuss over the garden and think about colors and timing, or I’d get excited to hear what everyone thought about a book. Now I look at those same things and it’s almost like they belong to someone I used to be, not to me now.

Sometimes I still go through the motions, or I tell myself I should care, but the feeling doesn’t really come. It’s like there’s an emptiness where the interest used to be, and it’s been pretty constant.
Do you find yourself blaming yourself or having negative thoughts about yourself, others, or the world because of what happened?

Yes… I do. More than I’d like to admit.

I keep going back over it in my head, over and over, like if I examine every little decision closely enough I’ll find the one place where I could have changed it. I tell myself, if I had chosen a different route that day, maybe we wouldn’t have been at that crossing. Or if I had pushed harder about how unsafe it was there — complained more, written more letters, made more noise — maybe something would have been done before she was killed.

I know part of me understands that I didn’t make that driver do what they did. But then another part of me says, “You should have known. You should have prevented it.” And that thought is just… it’s cruel, but it comes anyway.

And then I get furious all over again. At the driver, absolutely. But also at the town, because that crossing never felt safe to me, and now it feels like everyone just let it happen. Like the danger was sitting there in plain sight and nobody cared enough until it was too late. So yes, I blame myself, and I blame them, and sometimes it makes the whole world feel careless and dangerous.

inference_history.note: The patient's description of intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, and strong emotional and physical reactions to reminders of the traumatic event align with PTSD criteria. Further evaluation of symptom duration and severity will determine the specific subtype.

The patient's symptoms of re-experiencing the traumatic event through intrusive thoughts and flashbacks, avoidance of reminders, and heightened reactivity to trauma-related stimuli confirm the presence of a trauma-related disorder. This narrows the focus to subtypes of PTSD (F43.1) with the exclusion of F43.10 (Post-traumatic stress disorder, unspecified) due to the clarity of the patient's ongoing symptoms, making F43.11 (Post-traumatic stress disorder, acute) and F43.12 (Post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic) the most relevant candidates.

The patient has confirmed persistent feelings of emptiness and lack of interest that have lasted most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. This supports the presence of a depressive component in addition to PTSD symptoms. Both F43.11 (Post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic) and F43.12 (Complex post-traumatic stress disorder) remain viable candidates as they account for ongoing emotional and behavioral responses to trauma, including depressive symptoms, intrusive memories, avoidance, and hypervigilance.
